author: Caesar
rationale: The classic intermediate prose author. Direct, narrative, military. Caesar's commentaries are the most widely read Latin prose after Cicero.
description: You will read all of Book I of Caesar's Gallic War: the campaigns of 58 BCE, including the migrations of the Helvetians, the defeat of Ariovistus, and the winter quarters. Caesar writes in a plain, direct style; his sentences are shorter and more regular than Cicero's, but no less effective. This is the Latin that generations of schoolchildren learned first, and for good reason.
learning_outcomes: Read and translate all of De Bello Gallico Book I (c. 16,000 words) with notes.
Recognize Caesar's characteristic style: indirect statement, ablative absolutes, purpose clauses.
Translate any fifty-word passage from Book I at sight without notes.
Discuss Caesar's self-presentation and political aims in writing.

weekly_plan.focus: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa. Geography and the three divisions of Gaul.
The Gallic tribes appeal to Caesar against Ariovistus.
Caesar summons Ariovistus to a conference.
The defeat of Ariovistus and the German retreat.
Winter quarters and the placement of legions.
Read the first half again at speed.
Read the second half again at speed.
Read the entire book aloud in two sittings.
Sight translation practice from random passages.

recommended_resources: Edwards, H.J. (trans.), Caesar: The Gallic War (Loeb Classical Library)
Hammond, Carolyn, Caesar: De Bello Gallico (Oxford Classical Texts)
Raaflaub, Kurt A. & Ramsey, John T., Reconstructing the Roman Republic: An Ancient Political Culture and Modern Research
capstone_prep: In the final two weeks, focus on sight translation. Take random fifty-word passages from Book I and translate them without notes. Practice recognizing Caesar's patterns: indirect statement, temporal clauses, ablative absolutes. On the capstone exam you will see one passage from Book I that you have not prepared.
